Former tailscalar here and now someone managing tailscale at an org.

Having done my own review of the vulns and the fixes as they are landing in github, its pretty clear to me that this only affects situations where you use ACLs to permit ssh into a node (via tailscale ssh, not via opensshd), but dont give a path to sudoers/root.

If a user had no SSH access and/or connectivity to a vulnerable node, none of these vulns give them access.

However, if you have a vulnerable tailscaled and you give ssh access as some non-root account/privs, then yes, these vulns are relevant as theres now known privilege escalations that give access beyond some specific user account.

Not trying to play down the vuln (its important), but its not a free-for-all RCE that some ppl are acting like it is.

Calling it “tailworm” feels like alarmism to promote their find more.

Would only show worm behavior if machines within the tailnet had the right settings and also were members of other tailnets with those settings but then it would require someone in that tailnet to have another tailnet with the right settings…

It’s far fetched.

But a large portion of Tailscale users should be software engineering professionals, so a lot of the time, people use Tailscale just for SSH. I personally feel the impact is still quite big, especially since SSH leads directly to control of the server.

Do you use tailscale ssh but either dont have sudo, or don't permit login as root?

If all your tailscale-ssh ACLs allow you into an account with sudo, or allow you into root, theres no impact (you cant do anything with these vulns you couldnt do a month ago). Thats the nuance I'm trying to get across (admittedly my english is bad).

On the majority of nodes I provide Tailscale SSH access to, it's as root or a user with passwordless sudo. It's being used for admin access. So yeah, on those it doesn't matter as much.

There are a handful which restrict users to their own user accounts. But it's on dev server with friendly devs, so even for that use case it's not really the end of the world.

I'm sure our infosec folks are going to demand that we upgrade everywhere, however.
Engineers use vanilla SSH for SSH, Tailscale SSH is more focused on enterprise stuff where you can have an audit trail of all commands executed and enforce ACLs.

I’ve used tailscale in quite a few jobs now and not one have we used tailscale ssh. Call us old school or whatever but at my current place of employment we provision ssh keys on a box with ansible and just use regular old ssh over the tailnet, not tailscale ssh
Tailscale SSH is different than doing SSH with Tailscale

My gut feel is that you're correct but presumably they do have a decent number of proper corporate customers or none of these features would exist in the first place.

My sample size is small but nearly everyone I talked to uses basically zero of the tailscale advanced features. The VPN, the tunneling, and the internal IP/DNS - nothing else. And the same is true for headscale and netbird.

It's just basic economics. This is true for any service that offers a freemium model and you have more than 1,000 total users.

Any time you provide a free tier it's going to have more users than the paid options. I'm sure they make a decent chunk of revenue from the paid users so it's not a comment on earnings/economic feasibility specifically.

I use tailnet as a vpn and ssh into my server via the tailnet, but I dont use tailscale ssh the product. I think most people fall into this bucket.

Of course it should be taken seriously, but this topic is also piggy backing off of 7 days straight of non stop viral engagement farming on X after php2shell, where people we're farming likes by just posting stuff like

"YoU ThInK PhP2ShELl iS BaD JuST WaIt unTiL TaIlScAlE get HaCkED, ThIS JuSt ThE BeGiNNiNG oF a CybeR ReCKoNiNG"

To farm FUD from normies. Which of course led researchers who were working on tailscale vulns to take advantage of that algorithmic attention as well and talk about their research.

Like Im pretty sure we knew about this vuln for 3 days now, or atleast that it was responsibly disclosed (and not being used in the wild).

I personally use openssh, but someone else may use tailscale SSH.

I am fairly glad I have stuck with stock OpenSSH that ships with Linux. This incident proves I am glad with that choice.

Over the decades, I have maintained remote access through port forwarding on my router - at one point in 2008 I put SSH on port 80 so I could access it from the restricted wifi network at the hospital my grandmother was at. I have also used openvpn. I have also used cloudflare tunnels. But in the end, I always connect to hardened openssh with key only authentication.
Your use of OpenSSH in a single private network does not equate in any way or form using and distributing a non-ACL managed SSH client.

Clearly, but of all the ways to manage authorized keys on a fleet of endpoints was this particular methodology the only or best? Were there other ways to activate and deactivate keys without introducing the same complexity and brittleness. Clearly the ACL methodology provided a false sense of security in this instance in the presence of this bug.

What „all“ the ways exist?

Tailscale is also neither complex or brittle. It is insanely straightforward and very robust.

sounds like just adding complexity over traditional method of OpenSSH + key distribution (either via configuration management or ldap)

and now, bugs

Adding complexity would imply you're doing both. In this case it would be more correct to say you're trading the complexity of key distribution and access control via keys for the complexity introduced by tailscale ssh.

No, it doesn't sound like it. Tailscale reduces complexity. It literally is key distribution with an ACL.

I work at a finance org with hundreds of engineers and thousands of technical users. You cannot be compliant with finance compliance frameworks using OpenSSH without audits and traceability and some source of identity management. That is exactly what Tailscale (or an alternative product) provides.

> and now, bugs

If you do it yourself, you now own that software entirely. Your comment lacks understanding of the complexity of real world scenarios.

You just need to implement an SSH CA. You can roll your own. Vault has an enterprise one. StepCA is suitable for smaller orgs.

All the benefit of the core SSH protocol as it's just key signing. It's honestly underrated.

How does having an SSH CA help you roll out detailed access to hosts/ports/services with fine grained permissions via access control lists derived from your identity provider? How do you make sure you're giving out least privileges with a compliant onboarding/offboarding and audit process? That is where the real meat is.

If you've solved all these problems yourself at your org: congrats, you re-implemented Tailscale with a bespoke solution that takes orders of magnitudes more $ to maintain and audit regularly than just buying an industry trusted solution.

Tailscale is, all things concerned, really cheap. It costs less at my large org than a single engineer. Doing it ourselves would take a team. Maybe two. Once again, HM primarily comments from a naive engineer's perspective, not from a leadership view.
yep, this was obvious from day one.

Somehow I don't think it's a good idea to let Tailscale handle service authentication at all. It's supposed to be an additional security layer around existing infrastructure and services.

SSH key management at scale is a pain. You have to use certificate based SSH at least. In contrast, tailscale allows you to manage remote login at the same layer as connectivity, with better logging and alerting.
Sure, it is a difficult problem. But letting Tailscale handle both VPN and Auth at the same time might be a problem too.
This was a decision I made in my old job, seems to be proved correct.

It is massively more complex than say Wireguard, because it was developed with "everything and kitchen sink approach", and even the standard de facto authors, Cisco, took good 20 years to stop having IPSec related vulnerability every few months (hell we just had one this year in Linux IIRC)

That doesn’t really help much if you want to connect an arbitrary number of nodes to eachother (each of which is potentially on an entirely different LAN), does it? That’s really the whole point of Tailscale.

Taildrop only works with devices that are yours, i.e. you can't send or receive anything from a device that's either tagged or owned by someone else. The only way malware is getting onto your NAS (via Taildrop) is if you're the one sending it there.

My Tailscale RCE[1] in 2022 involved forcing a device onto an attacker-controlled control plane, at which point your device is no longer "yours", and the fact that Taildrop is implemented in your client binary can be exploited. Chaining the bug to RCE would not have been possible against an ideal Tailscale with only the core feature set.

[1]: https://web.archive.org/web/20221222120703/https://emily.id....

Re: Your question. Taildrop only works between devices in the same account. So if you don't put low trust devices in the same account as your NAS this is mitigated.

Tailnet owner may not trust all their devices to the same extent. Here is a concrete example.

I install tailscale on my cloud vps which I use for downloading torrents. I want my laptop to talk to this node, but I don't want this vm talk to my laptop, which is the whole purpose of ACLs. My ACL is deny by default, so that is great and easy to set. But now this node can still send arbitrary files to my laptop. If I don't remember to tag it, I'm vulnerable. If I do, there is still a window that this node can send me files until I tag it (I can't install tailscale to a tag).

Sending a file otherwise normally requires an app listening to a port, so taildrop permissions should be same as network permissions set by ACL.

BTW, last year or so tailscale advertised a position for someone to manage complexity of tailscale. Founder was talking about this issue. They seem to be aware of the problem.

Tags are a key part of managing ACLs. If you're concerned about an untrustworthy node on your tailnet, use tags. Even if you forget to add a tag to a newly added node (API keys can be set to automatically assume a tag when used fwiw), if your other devices are tagged then they're ineligible for taildrop.

I don't see the reason for Tailscale instead of plain old simple Wireguard, it's WG under the hood anyway.

+1

I am a relatively old school engineer. When building a bricks and mortar business recently I kept hearing about tailscale for remote access. Looked and saw it was just a wrapper over wireguard. I immediately went aha, there's a solid underlying project without the risk of something over the top trying to make life easier for people unwilling or unable to manage their own systems. Went with a direct wireguard on opnsense approach.

Bamn, proved right today.

Wireguard is perfectly elegant and maintainable as it is for me, and a wonderful improvement on traditional site to site VPNs.

This exactly. All the extra stuff Tailscale provides buys convenience, but increases complexity, the attack surface of the stack, and adds commercial components to an otherwise open protocol. Call me old fashioned but I will keep managing keys manually.

I like Tailascale as a product but I decided to move my homelab to plain WireGuard.

using wireguard is awesome, but I wouldn't say deploying and maintaining it lacks complexity exactly. and you didn't get rid of attack surface, you just made it your responsibility ;)
Always is your responsibility even with tailscale. Now it is his responsibility without tailscale.

Attack surface almost entirely goes away if you just require a good port knock first! I do that with my protection SSH servers and it works just fine. Also prevents anyone from knowing there even is an SSH server there. Or any server if it doesn't respond to pings either, and only uses reverse tunnels to accept public connections
Wireguard doesn’t respond to malformed packets or handshakes from unknown devices by design.
Oh, awesome!
Is there a way to automate port knocks in your .ssh/config? I think that’s the main reason why I haven’t added it to my home server.

Port knocking is idiotic and amounts to Biff Tannen's "only I know how to start this car".

Dunno, in combination with having an up to date system following best practices, port knocking is probably going to save you when bots start scanning the internet with the next SSH 0day. Any amount of friction will cause the bots to move to the next IP address.
Just moving SSH off a default port gets you 98% there.
An attacker only has to get lucky once, so while I do put SSH on a non-default port too, it's not enough to avoid attacks on its own.
I mostly do it to quiet down the noise from the non-stop bots and scanners.
Being off the IPv4 space completely can be even more effective at that, FWIW, but that can have other issues. Only feasible for some!
LLMs port knock for redteam scans. Have for a long time.
My knock for SSH was 20 ports within 2 seconds. knockd resets the sequence if you hit any of its ports out of order. I generated the sequence with a CSPRNG.
That's not a knock, it's a password :-)
I mean, it suffers from some of the same issues with knocks, like being replayable. Wonder if anyone's come up with a TOTP-like thing for port knocks, where the code changes every little bit...

Yes something like that has been done, the solution uses asymmetric cryptography instead of symmetric and it protects the entire communication stream instead of just opening the gates - it's called Wireguard.

I jest, but you're describing authentication protocol which uses the UDP destination port field to carry each character of the "one time password" in a roundabout way. You could simply send 1 packet containing the password to the daemon.

I've never seen it used in the wild but apparently, it exists: https://github.com/mrash/fwknop

LOL'd at Wireguard, but I really miss Plan 9-style networking, where you can basically just scope VPNs to a subprocess rather than having to use some system wide network filter with split tunneling or whatever. Wireguard has huge usability issues due to that.

Reading the fwknop README is such a breath of fresh air, thank you for that treat. I hate AI-generated documentation so much.

To be quite honest, I just like the aesthetics of it.

I did this by hand before and it was hard and difficult to get right. Now I just tell AI and it does so perfectly, checks and verifies things. AI made life so easy.

"Should" and "shouldn't" are dependent on context. In this case, that somewhat depends on what the router you're using is, how much you trust it, and your ISP's configuration. Opening a port isn't an inherently insecure thing, it's a choice that you make while being aware of the tradeoffs between that port being exposed to the internet at large and wanting a given service to be available.
What's the advantage of adding a VPS to the mix?

Having a VPS gives you a static, non-shared, stable IP with a whois that doesn’t resolve to a residential ISP.

Lot’s of ISP have moved to CGNAT where port forwarding has become a nightmare. That’s one reason. You can look at it as if your router moved from your home behind a public CGNAT, dynamic, shared IP to a public non-shared, static, stable IP on the internet.

In a workplace setting, connecting to your residential IP will raise suspicions or alarms. That being said, if you go for a cheap VPS, it also might raise alarms. Maybe your 'VPS' should be with whichever cloud provider your employer goes with so you don’t even register as a blip.

It is added complexity, but it is really very simple. Using Wireguard, you connect from a always on server in your home to your VPS. Then, using Wireguard, you configure your laptop to always connect to your VPS. Any local LLM can generate the wg-quick config files in seconds.
